continuingVsTotal.title: Continuing vs. total net income
continuingVsTotal.content:
Net income (continuing ops) excludes any segment sold or being wound down; discontinued-ops profit is the result (trading profit plus any gain/loss on sale) of that segment up to disposal.

For Premier Investments: Premier sold its Apparel Brands retail segment (Just Jeans, Portmans, Jay Jays, Dotti, Jacqui E) to Myer, completing in FY2025. FY2024 and FY2025 both carry a large discontinued-ops line -- FY2025's total net income of $338.2m includes a $194.2m one-off discontinued-ops profit on top of $144.0m from continuing operations, so total net income overstates the run-rate earnings power of the retained business (Smiggle, Peter Alexander, and the Breville stake) by roughly 2.3x that year alone.

What to watch:

  • Continuing-ops net income is the right base for any forward multiple or DCF, not total net income in FY2024/FY2025
  • FY2026 has zero discontinued-ops profit -- the divestment is fully behind the numbers from here

associateProfit.title: Breville associate profit
associateProfit.content:
Under equity accounting, Premier books only its share of Breville's net profit as a single line -- Breville's revenue, costs and balance sheet are not consolidated into Premier's own statements.

For Premier Investments: Premier holds 25.2% of Breville Group (ASX: BRG), a listed small-appliance maker (Nespresso, Breville-branded kitchen products). This associate profit has grown from $13.1m in FY2015 to $34.4-42.4m in recent years and is a recurring, non-cash-until-dividend contributor to net income that sits outside the core retail (Smiggle, Peter Alexander) operating story -- it should be valued separately (e.g. at Breville's own market multiple on Premier's stake) rather than capitalised at the retail business's multiple.

What to watch:

  • Associate profit growth versus Breville's own reported NPAT (Premier's 25.2% share should track it)
  • Cash actually received as Breville dividends versus the accounted profit share (the gap builds up in the investment's carrying value, not in Premier's cash)

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Premier Investments Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Premier Investments Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Premier Investments Limited: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Premier Investments Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Premier Investments Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Premier Investments Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Premier Investments Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Premier Investments Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Premier Investments Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Premier Investments Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
